title: Consider plant botany during the placement of bee hives

lessons.title: Flowers that feed bees
lessons.html:
What bees get from plants

Honey bees live on two foods that come from flowers:

  • Nectar: a sweet liquid. Bees turn it into honey. It gives them energy.
  • Pollen: a fine powder made by the male part of the flower. It gives bees protein to feed young bees (brood).

Bees also need water every day, and some collect plant resin to make propolis, the glue of the hive.

Parts of a flower

  • Petals: the coloured parts that attract bees.
  • Stamens: the male parts that carry pollen.
  • Pistil: the female part in the middle that receives pollen and later makes seed or fruit.
  • Nectaries: small glands at the base of the flower that make nectar.

When a bee moves from flower to flower it carries pollen. This is called pollination. Many crops such as apples, pears, avocados, macadamias, sunflowers and pumpkins give better crops when bees pollinate them.

Good bee plants in South Africa

TypeExamples
TreesEucalyptus (bluegum), acacias, citrus, fruit trees
Field cropsSunflower, canola, lucerne in flower
Veld and fynbosAloes, proteas, ericas, wild flowers

Note that some plants such as certain eucalyptus species are controlled invader plants in some areas. Bees still use them, but you must not plant them without checking the rules.

lessons.title: Choosing a place for the hives
lessons.html:
Follow the flowers

Bees usually fly up to about two to three kilometres from the hive to find food, and further when food is scarce. The closer good flowers are, the less energy bees use and the more honey they store. Before you place hives, walk the area and look at what is flowering now and what will flower in the next weeks.

Flowering times

Different plants flower at different times of the year. A good beekeeper knows the flowering calendar of the area. For example, aloes flower in winter, citrus in spring, sunflower in summer. When one plant stops flowering, bees may have to be moved to another place or given help.

A good hive site has

  • Plenty of flowers with nectar and pollen within flying distance.
  • Clean water nearby, but not in a place that floods.
  • Shade in the hot afternoon and shelter from strong wind.
  • Hives off the ground on stands, protected from ants and honey badgers.
  • Easy access for the bakkie, but away from paths, houses, kraals and roads.

Places to avoid

  • Close to where people, children or animals walk or work. Bees can attack.
  • Fields that are sprayed with insecticides.
  • Wet, cold valleys and places with poor flowers.

On a crop farm, the farmer and beekeeper should agree where hives go and when.

lessons.title: Pesticides, poisonous plants and safety
lessons.html:
Protecting bees from sprays

Many insect sprays kill bees. Bees can die on the flowers or carry poison back to the hive. Agricultural remedies are controlled under Act 36 of 1947, and the label tells you whether a product is harmful to bees.

  • Find out the spray programme of the farm and neighbours before placing hives.
  • Ask that sprays are not used on flowering crops while bees are working, or are used late in the evening when bees are not flying, as the label allows.
  • Close or move hives if spraying cannot be avoided.
  • Report dead bees in front of the hive to your supervisor.

Plants that can cause problems

A few plants make nectar or honey that is not good for bees or people. If you are not sure, ask your supervisor or an experienced beekeeper. Never sell honey you are worried about.

Working safely near bees

  • Wear a bee suit, veil, gloves and boots when working with hives.
  • Use a smoker to keep bees calm.
  • Work slowly and do not stand in front of the hive entrance.
  • Know who on the team is allergic to stings. A person who has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or who collapses after stings needs emergency help immediately. Call for help and get them to a clinic or hospital at once.

For a normal sting, scrape the sting out with a fingernail or blade and move away from the hive.

Key points

  • Bees need nectar for energy, pollen for protein, and water every day.
  • Place hives within flying distance of good flowers and check the flowering calendar.
  • Give hives shade, water, wind shelter and keep them away from people and animals.
  • Agree on spray times so bees are not poisoned.
  • Severe reactions to stings are an emergency; get medical help at once.
